title: Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE 38th International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI). When Does Closed-Loop Curriculum Adaptation Help GRPO? An Analysis on Countdown

paper.title: Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE 38th International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI). When Does Closed-Loop Curriculum Adaptation Help GRPO? An Analysis on Countdown
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for
improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains
sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the
model’s current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO),
problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while
problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this
work, we introduce ClosedLoopGaussian , a lightweight adaptive
curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered
reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, ClosedLoopGaussian preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian
sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe
estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training
when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model
falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This
feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but
still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or
underlying GRPO optimizer. Experiments on symbolic arithmetic reasoning task
show that ClosedLoopGaussian improves exact-match accuracy over
vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains in
intermediate-difficulty regimes where group-relative learning signals are
most informative. Codes are available at https://github.com/yuvrajpant56/Closed_Loop_Curriculum .

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) [ 6 , 13 , 7 ] has become an important post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning behavior of large language models (LLMs). Instead of imitating fixed solution traces, an RLVR system samples candidate solutions, scores them with a verifier such as exact-answer matching or executable checks, and updates the policy toward higher-reward responses, improving performance on mathematical, programming, and symbolic reasoning tasks [ 6 , 7 ] . Group-relative methods such as GRPO further make RLVR practical by estimating advantages from multiple sampled responses to the same prompt, avoiding the need for a separately trained critic [ 11 ] , and have been applied beyond mathematical reasoning, for example to train generative judges [ 3 ] . Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed adaptive closed-loop curriculum framework. Despite this progress, GRPO remains highly sensitive to the difficulty of the problems selected for training. When a problem is too hard for the current policy, most rollouts fail, producing sparse rewards and little useful advantage signal [ 16 ] . When a problem is already too easy, sampled responses become uniformly correct, again reducing within-group reward variation. In both regimes the expensive rollout budget yields a weak gradient; indeed, Bae et al. [ 1 ] show formally that expected policy improvement is maximized on tasks of intermediate difficulty, where success probabilities have the highest variance. A family of methods therefore modifies the optimization or rollout procedure itself: DAPO filters and resamples prompts until each batch contains groups with non-zero reward variance [ 16 ] , GSPO changes the granularity of policy optimization [ 17 ] , and ShareGRPO improves the construction and reuse of group-relative learning signals [ 15 ] . These approaches improve how learning signals are extracted from sampled responses, but online filtering spends variable rollout cost per update. Curriculum learning addresses difficulty mismatch by organizing training from easier to harder tasks as competence develops [ 2 ] , and automatic curriculum methods select tasks from learning progress, competence estimates, or a learned teacher policy [ 5 , 8 , 9 ] . In reinforcement fine-tuning for reasoning, Parashar et al. [ 10 ] propose probabilistic easy-to-hard schedulers, including a Gaussian schedule (E2H-G) that smoothly shifts training mass across ordered difficulty buckets. These schedules are open-loop : their pace and spread are fixed before training and followed regardless of the model’s actual learning trajectory. This is fragile when progress varies across seeds and difficulty levels; a model may learn faster than expected, stall on intermediate tasks, or regress on earlier skills while the curriculum continues to advance. Closer to our setting, a recent line of adaptive schedulers closes this gap from observed training signals: ADaRFT(Adaptive Curriculum Reinforcement Finetuning) steers a scalar target difficulty from recent rewards [ 12 ] , DUMP schedules sampling across data distributions with a bandit rule over advantage magnitudes [ 14 ] , and SEC(Self-Evolving Curriculum) learn a task-selection policy alongside training [ 4 ] . These methods demonstrate the value of matching training tasks to current capability, but they generally represent curriculum state through either a task-selection policy or a single target-difficulty variable, which does not explicitly separate two distinct curriculum decisions: how quickly to advance toward harder tasks, and how broadly to rehearse previously encountered difficulties. The central question of this paper is: Can a curriculum scheduler use feedback from the model’s own learning trajectory to synchronize task selection with current capability, and does this closed-loop control improve reinforcement fine-tuning over a fixed easy-to-hard schedule? We answer this question with ClosedLoopGaussian , a closed-loop curriculum scheduler for GRPO-style reasoning post-training. Particularly, the paper makes the following three key contributions: • Algorithm. ClosedLoopGaussian , a closed-loop scheduler that adapts the pace β t \beta_{t} and spread σ t \sigma_{t} of a Gaussian easy-to-hard sampler from per-difficulty pass rates. • Analysis. Formalizing curriculum scheduling for group-relative reinforcement learning as a compute-allocation problem, decoupling control of rehearsal breadth. • Evaluation. A four-seed comparison against vanilla GRPO and a fixed open-loop curriculum on Countdown, under an identical rollout budget, showing improved average accuracy, where group-relative learning signals are most informative.

sections.heading: II Methodology
sections.text: ClosedLoopGaussian is a closed-loop curriculum scheduler for GRPO-style reasoning post-training that changes only the distribution from which training prompts are sampled, while leaving the underlying model, verifier, reward function, and optimizer unchanged. At each step, a Gaussian sampler assigns probabilities over ordered difficulty buckets, while periodic probe evaluations estimate bucket-wise accuracy. A feedback controller then adjusts the curriculum pace β t \beta_{t} and spread σ t \sigma_{t} so that training can progress toward harder problems, slow when performance lags, or broaden rehearsal when earlier difficulties regress. A single scheduler object is shared by the sampler, trainer, and probe evaluator, so updates to β t \beta_{t} or σ t \sigma_{t} affect the next sampled batch. From a compute-allocation perspective, the sampler determines how the fixed rollout budget is distributed across difficulty levels. The controller therefore adapts β t \beta_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} to reallocate training compute according to the model’s observed competence. Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline. The remainder of this section describes the difficulty buckets (§ II-A ), Gaussian sampler (§ II-B ), and probe-driven closed-loop controller (§ II-C ).

sections.heading: II-A Ordered Difficulty Space
sections.text: Each Countdown instance provides a set of input numbers and a target integer, and requires an arithmetic expression over + + , − - , × \times , ÷ \div that uses each input number exactly once and evaluates to the target. The data provide fixed ordered difficulty groups indexed by n ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } n\in\{2,3,4,5\} , the number of input operands in the instance; larger n n increases the combinatorial search space and is empirically harder for the policy. We denote these preassigned groups by 𝒟 0 , … , 𝒟 K − 1 \mathcal{D}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{K-1} . The curriculum does not infer or relabel difficulty: at each step it samples a bucket k ∼ p t k\sim p_{t} and then samples an example uniformly from 𝒟 k \mathcal{D}_{k} . Exact-answer correctness is determined independently by the unchanged Countdown verifier.

sections.heading: II-B Gaussian Curriculum Sampler
sections.text: The sampler follows the same Gaussian easy-to-hard form as the fixed E2H-G baseline [ 10 ] , which keeps the sampling family fixed and makes feedback the primary design difference between the two arms. At optimizer step t t with total optimizer budget T T , the curriculum center is x t = ( t T − 1 ) β t ​ ( K − 1 ) x_{t}\;=\;\left(\frac{t}{T-1}\right)^{\beta_{t}}\,(K-1) (1) and bucket k k is sampled with probability p t ​ ( k ) = exp ⁡ ( − ( k − x t ) 2 2 ​ σ t 2 ) + p min ∑ j = 0 K − 1 [ exp ⁡ ( − ( j − x t ) 2 2 ​ σ t 2 ) + p min ] p_{t}(k)\;=\;\frac{\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{(k-x_{t})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right)+p_{\min}}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\left[\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{(j-x_{t})^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right)+p_{\min}\right]} (2) The pace β t \beta_{t} controls how quickly x t x_{t} migrates from the easiest bucket toward the hardest: smaller β t \beta_{t} advances the curriculum sooner, larger β t \beta_{t} holds it on easier material longer. The spread σ t \sigma_{t} controls rehearsal breadth: larger σ t \sigma_{t} flattens the distribution so neighboring buckets stay in the rollout mix. The additive floor p min > 0 p_{\min}>0 is applied to each unnormalized weight before normalization, guaranteeing every bucket retains nonzero probability; this keeps the hardest bucket from being starved entirely early in training while its share stays negligible until the controller deems it worthwhile. Unlike ( 1 )–( 2 ) with β t \beta_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} held constant at predefined reference values for all t t ; the proposed method instead adapts these parameters over time.

sections.heading: II-C Closed-Loop Curriculum Controller
sections.text: The controller closes the loop between the curriculum clock and the model’s observed competence using a fixed, non-learned feedback rule based on two inexpensive, interpretable signals. It remains anchored to the reference trajectory, reverting to the open-loop baseline when no corrective signal is present, and can be viewed as an RLVR-specific form of learning-progress-based automatic curriculum learning [ 5 , 9 ] .

sections.heading: Probe evaluation and calibration
sections.text: Every Δ = 100 \Delta=100 optimizer steps, the controller greedily evaluates a fixed, pre-cached set of 100 100 held-out examples per difficulty bucket using the unchanged Countdown verifier, producing 𝐀 = ( A 0 , … , A K − 1 ) \mathbf{A}=(A_{0},\ldots,A_{K-1}) . This probe is the only additional GPU computation introduced by ClosedLoopGaussian ; indicative timing is reported in § III . Controller parameters were coarsely calibrated to keep feedback responsive but bounded: h h and ℓ \ell were chosen from reference mid-training pass rates, while gains and clipping ranges were set conservatively to limit deviation from the E2H-G reference. Settings were then frozen before the reported comparison; seed 42 was used during calibration.

sections.heading: III-A Experimental Setup
sections.text: Model and Optimization. All experiments use meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with LoRA fine-tuning. LoRA uses rank r = 32 r=32 , scale α LoRA = 64 \alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}=64 , and dropout 0.05 0.05 . Training runs for 1,600 1{,}600 optimizer steps with a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , cosine decay, and a 0.03 0.03 warm-up ratio. The per-device batch size is 4 4 with 4 4 gradient-accumulation steps. GRPO samples 4 4 generations per prompt with KL coefficient 0.001 0.001 and maximum gradient norm 1.0 1.0 . Generation and Probing. The maximum prompt and completion lengths are 1,024 1{,}024 and 192 192 tokens, respectively. Training generations use temperature 0.7 0.7 and top- p = 1.0 p=1.0 . Controller probes are performed every Δ = 100 \Delta=100 optimizer steps using a fixed set of 100 100 examples from each difficulty bucket and greedy decoding. Periodic probing introduces additional inference cost; in one representative run, ClosedLoopGaussian required 12.94 h versus 11.49 h for Fixed E2H-G and 10.82 h for GRPO, although these single-run timings are indicative only. Controller Configuration. The controller uses reference values β ref = 0.50 \beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.50 and σ ref = 0.50 \sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.50 , with probability floor p min = 0.01 p_{\min}=0.01 . The controller variables are bounded by β ∈ [ 0.35 , 0.70 ] \beta\in[0.35,0.70] and σ ∈ [ 0.40 , 0.80 ] \sigma\in[0.40,0.80] . The update parameters are η β = η σ = 0.50 \eta_{\beta}=\eta_{\sigma}=0.50 , λ β = λ σ = 0.30 \lambda_{\beta}=\lambda_{\sigma}=0.30 , and c fgt = 2.0 c_{\mathrm{fgt}}=2.0 . For buckets 𝒟 0 , … , 𝒟 3 \mathcal{D}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{3} , the upper and lower thresholds are h = ( 0.60 , 0.30 , 0.15 , 0.08 ) h=(0.60,0.30,0.15,0.08) and ℓ = ( 0.30 , 0.10 , 0.04 , 0.02 ) \ell=(0.30,0.10,0.04,0.02) , respectively. The corresponding upward and downward weighting vectors are w up = ( 0.25 , 0.75 , 1.00 , 1.00 ) w^{\mathrm{up}}=(0.25,0.75,1.00,1.00) and w dn = ( 1.00 , 1.00 , 0.75 , 0.25 ) w^{\mathrm{dn}}=(1.00,1.00,0.75,0.25) . Forgetting is monitored over ℰ = { 0 , 1 } \mathcal{E}=\{0,1\} , corresponding to buckets 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} and 𝒟 1 \mathcal{D}_{1} .

sections.heading: III-B Accuracy Across Difficulty Levels
sections.text: Across four seeds, average exact-match accuracy is 42.4 % ± 14.0 % 42.4\%\pm 14.0\% for ClosedLoopGaussian , 35.0 % ± 11.4 % 35.0\%\pm 11.4\% for Fixed E2H-G, and 26.4 % ± 21.6 % 26.4\%\pm 21.6\% for GRPO (Table I ). Across difficulty levels, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN achieves mean accuracies of 82.7%, 52.3%, 23.2%, and 11.5% for n = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 n=2,3,4,5 , respectively, compared with 73.1%, 40.8%, 16.3%, and 9.7% for Fixed E2H-G. ClosedLoopGaussian exceeds Fixed E2H-G on all four reported seeds, but the across-seed dispersion is large relative to the mean gaps; with only n = 4 n=4 seeds, the comparison does not support a statistical-significance claim and is therefore interpreted descriptively. The largest mean gains over Fixed E2H-G occur at difficulty n = 3 n=3 ( 52.3 % 52.3\% vs. 40.8 % 40.8\% ) and n = 4 n=4 ( 23.2 % 23.2\% vs. 16.3 % 16.3\% ), consistent with adaptation being most useful where rollouts are neither uniformly correct nor uniformly incorrect. Each bucket contains 250 250 evaluation problems, so one example corresponds to 0.4 0.4 percentage points; small differences at n = 5 n=5 therefore represent only a few examples and should not be overinterpreted. sections.heading: III-C Controller Dynamics: When Does Adaptation Help?
sections.text: Figure 2 traces β t \beta_{t} , σ t \sigma_{t} , u β u_{\beta} , and n = 3 n=3 probe accuracy across all four seeds. The first probe at step 100 100 shows near-floor accuracy beyond the easiest bucket, producing a mildly negative u β u_{\beta} and a small increase in β t \beta_{t} above its 0.5 0.5 reference. After warm-up, two qualitative regimes emerge. On seeds 42 42 , 43 43 , and 1 1 , n = 3 n=3 probe accuracy rises, u β u_{\beta} becomes positive, and β t \beta_{t} decreases toward approximately 0.35 0.35 – 0.40 0.40 , shifting progression toward harder buckets; σ t \sigma_{t} remains near its reference with only modest widening. Seed 43 43 shows the strongest acceleration and the highest final accuracy, while seed 1 1 exhibits a transient mid-training dip before returning to the acceleration regime. Seed 44 44 follows a different trajectory: n = 3 n=3 competence remains low, u β u_{\beta} returns to zero after step 200 200 , and β t \beta_{t} relaxes near the reference, while forgetting on easier buckets widens σ t \sigma_{t} to approximately 0.63 0.63 . This near-reference β t \beta_{t} is the intended reference-anchoring behavior when no pace-adjustment signal is present. The fixed controller therefore exhibits either accelerated progression or increased rehearsal depending on the observed probe trajectory. As a single-seed auxiliary analysis, seed 43 43 sampler logs show that the closed-loop schedule assigns 6.45 6.45 percentage points more sampling mass to n = 5 n=5 than Fixed E2H-G, with the shift drawn primarily from n = 3 n=3 and n = 4 n=4 . Notably, n = 3 n=3 accuracy improves despite receiving less n = 3 n=3 training exposure, suggesting that the gain cannot be explained simply by sampling that bucket more frequently. Dashed grey lines mark the reference values ( β ref = σ ref = 0.5 \beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.5 , u β = 0 u_{\beta}=0 ). Seeds 42 42 / 43 43 / 1 1 move ahead of pace and the controller accelerates the curriculum ( β t ↓ \beta_{t}\!\downarrow ); seed 44 44 never gets ahead, u β u_{\beta} stays at zero, and the controller instead widens the distribution ( σ t ↑ \sigma_{t}\!\uparrow ) to counter forgetting.

sections.heading: III-D Diagnostic Sensitivity to Controller Authority
sections.text: Seed 43 43 is examined because it exhibits the largest controller movement, making sensitivity to controller authority easiest to observe. This seed was selected after inspecting the controller trajectories, so the analysis is post hoc and is reported as a diagnostic rather than a representative ablation. On this seed, locking σ = 0.50 \sigma=0.50 reduces average accuracy from 58.9 58.9 to 26.2 26.2 , indicating that spread adaptation can matter for this trajectory. Pace-bound changes also produce substantial variation, with the default [ 0.35 , 0.70 ] [0.35,0.70] band outperforming both tighter and wider alternatives; this band was fixed before the reported runs (§ II-C ) and was not selected on the basis of these evaluation results. Because this diagnostic uses one selected seed and omits the complementary β \beta -locked/ σ \sigma -active condition, it does not establish an average contribution of σ \sigma or a causal decomposition of pace and spread.

sections.heading: III-E Seed-Dependent Stability
sections.text: The large standard deviations in Table I are consistent with training instability in the underlying GRPO optimization rather than by the curriculum. Vanilla GRPO is the least stable arm: it collapses to near-floor accuracy on two of the four seeds ( 44 44 and 1 1 , both 7.7 % 7.7\% ) while reaching 43 43 – 47 % 47\% on the other two, so its variance is bimodal rather than Gaussian and its mean of 26.4 % 26.4\% should be read with that in mind. These two seeds are separate runs with their own output directories and independently written checkpoints; their identical per-bucket accuracies reflect two runs reaching the same near-floor outcome, not a duplicated result entry. The curriculum arms avoided near-floor outcomes on the same initializations: Fixed E2H-G never falls below 19.2 % 19.2\% , and ClosedLoopGaussian never below 25.1 % 25.1\% . We therefore treat seed 44 44 not as an outlier to be averaged away but as a documented stability observation, and seed 1 1 shows the same effect for GRPO a second time: closed-loop adaptation provides a measure of robustness to an unfavorable optimization trajectory precisely because its pace and spread react to the model’s deteriorating competence. At the same time, we are explicit that with four seeds on a single 3 3 B model and a single task, these results give a consistent ordering and a mechanistic account , not a tight quantitative estimate of the expected gain.

sections.heading: IV Limitations and Future Directions
sections.text: This study focuses on a controlled setting: a single 3 3 B model (Llama-3.2-3B with LoRA), a single task (Countdown), and four seeds. The broader model, task, and seed coverage would further refine quantitative estimates of the expected gain, especially given the seed-to-seed variation observed in § III-E . Direct experimental comparisons with adaptive curricula such as AdaRFT, DUMP, and SEC are also left for future work. The controller’s effectiveness also depends on the choice of thresholds and control gains. Controller thresholds, gains, and bounds are manually calibrated; overly strict settings can cause curriculum deadlock, although the reference-anchored bounded design mitigates this failure mode. Future work should expand seed and domain coverage, compare directly with adaptive-curriculum baselines, and automate controller calibration from training signals.

sections.heading: V Conclusion
sections.text: This work studied when closed-loop curriculum adaptation improves reinforcement fine-tuning for LLM reasoning. We introduced ClosedLoopGaussian , a feedback-driven curriculum scheduler for GRPO that treats training-time data selection as an adaptive decision problem. Rather than changing the reward function, model architecture, or GRPO optimizer, ClosedLoopGaussian reallocates a fixed rollout budget across difficulty buckets using periodic probe estimates of per-bucket accuracy. It achieved higher mean exact-match accuracy than fixed E2H-G and vanilla GRPO across four reported seeds, although seed-to-seed variation is substantial. More broadly, this study highlights the value of decision-guided training mechanisms that improve reasoning by changing how compute is allocated, rather than by increasing model size or redesigning the optimizer, establishing closed-loop curriculum scheduling as a lightweight and transparent component for building more efficient AI training systems.

When Does Closed-Loop Curriculum Adaptation Help GRPO? An Analysis on Countdown Yuv Raj Pant ∗ \ast , Moshiur Rahman Tonmoy † {\dagger} , and Kaiqun Fu ∗ \ast Affiliation: ∗ \ast Department of Computer Science, Texas Christian University † {\dagger} Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Texas A&M University - Kingsville {yuv.raj.pant, k.fu}@tcu.edu, moshiur_rahman.tonmoy@students.tamuk.edu Abstract Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the model’s current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this work, we introduce ClosedLoopGaussian , a lightweight adaptive curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, ClosedLoopGaussian preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or underlying GRPO optimizer. Experiments on symbolic arithmetic reasoning task show that ClosedLoopGaussian improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains in intermediate-difficulty regimes where group-relative learning signals are most informative. Codes are available at https://github.com/yuvrajpant56/Closed_Loop_Curriculum . I Introduction Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) [ 6 , 13 , 7 ] has become an important post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning behavior of large language models (LLMs). Instead of imitating fixed solution traces, an RLVR system samples candidate solutions, scores them with a verifier such as exact-answer matching or executable checks, and updates the policy toward higher-reward responses, improving performance on mathematical, programming, and symbolic reasoning tasks [ 6 , 7 ] . Group-relative methods such as GRPO further make RLVR practical by estimating advantages from multiple sampled responses to the same prompt, avoiding the need for a separately trained critic [ 11 ] , and have been applied beyond mathematical reasoning, for example to train generative judges [ 3 ] . Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed adaptive closed-loop curriculum framework. Despite this progress, GRPO remains highly sensitive to the difficulty of the problems selected for training. When a problem is too hard for the current policy, most rollouts fail, producing sparse rewards and little useful advantage signal [ 16 ] . When a problem is already too easy, sampled responses become uniformly correct, again reducing within-group reward variation. In both regimes the expensive rollout budget yields a weak gradient; indeed, Bae et al. [ 1 ] show formally that expected policy improvement is maximized on tasks of intermediate difficulty, where success probabilities have the highest variance. A family of methods therefore modifies the optimization or rollout procedure itself: DAPO filters and resamples prompts until each batch contains groups with non-zero reward variance [ 16 ] , GSPO changes the granularity of policy optimization [ 17 ] , and ShareGRPO improves the construction and reuse of group-relative learning signals [ 15 ] . These approaches improve how learning signals are extracted from sampled responses, but online filtering spends variable rollout cost per update. Curriculum learning addresses difficulty mismatch by organizing training from easier to harder tasks as competence develops [ 2 ] , and automatic curriculum methods select tasks from learning progress, competence estimates, or a learned teacher policy [ 5 , 8 , 9 ] . In reinforcement fine-tuning for reasoning, Parashar et al. [ 10 ] propose probabilistic easy-to-hard schedulers, including a Gaussian schedule (E2H-G) that smoothly shifts training mass across ordered difficulty buckets. These schedules are open-loop : their pace and spread are fixed before training and followed regardless of the model’s actual learning trajectory. This is fragile when progress varies across seeds and difficulty levels; a model may learn faster than expected, stall on intermediate tasks, or regress on earlier skills while the curriculum continues to advance. Closer to our setting, a recent line of adaptive schedulers closes this gap from observed training signals: ADaRFT(Adaptive Curriculum Reinforcement Finetuning) steers a scalar target difficulty from recent rewards [ 12 ] , DUMP schedules sampling across data distributions with a bandit rule over advantage magnitudes [ 14 ] , and SEC(Self-Evolving Curriculum) learn a task-selection policy alongside training [ 4 ] . These methods demonstrate the value of matching training tasks to current capability, but they generally represent curriculum state through either a task-selection policy or a single target-difficulty variable, which does not explicitly separate two distinct curriculum decisions: how quickly to advance toward harder tasks, and how broadly to rehearse previously encountered difficulties. The central question of this paper is: Can a curriculum scheduler use feedback from the model’s own learning trajectory to synchronize task selection with current capability, and does this closed-loop control improve reinforcement fine-tuning over a fixed easy-to-hard schedule? We answer this question with ClosedLoopGaussian , a closed-loop curriculum scheduler for GRPO-style reasoning post-training. Particularly, the paper makes the following three key contributions: • Algorithm. ClosedLoopGaussian , a closed-loop scheduler that adapts the pace β t \beta_{t} and spread σ t \sigma_{t} of a Gaussian easy-to-hard sampler from per-difficulty pass rates. • Analysis. Formalizing curriculum scheduling for group-relative reinforcement learning as a compute-allocation problem, decoupling control of rehearsal breadth. • Evaluation. A four-seed comparison against vanilla GRPO and a fixed open-loop curriculum on Countdown, under an identical rollout budget, showing improved average accuracy, where group-relative learning signals are most informative. II Methodology ClosedLoopGaussian is a closed-loop curriculum scheduler for GRPO-style reasoning post-training that changes only the distribution from which training prompts are sampled, while leaving the underlying model, verifier, reward function, and optimizer unchanged. At each step, a Gaussian sampler assigns probabilities over ordered difficulty buckets, while periodic probe evaluations estimate bucket-wise accuracy. A feedback controller then adjusts the curriculum pace β t \beta_{t} and spread σ t \sigma_{t} so that training can progress toward harder problems, slow when performance lags, or broaden rehearsal when earlier difficulties regress. A single scheduler object is shared by the sampler, trainer, and probe evaluator, so updates to β t \beta_{t} or σ t \sigma_{t} affect the next sampled batch. From a compute-allocation perspective, the sampler determines how the fixed rollout budget is distributed across difficulty levels. The controller therefore adapts β t \beta_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} to reallocate training compute according to the model’s observed competence. Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline. The remainder of this section describes the difficulty buckets (§ II-A ), Gaussian sampler (§ II-B ), and probe-driven closed-loop controller (§ II-C ). II-A Ordered Difficulty Space Each Countdown instance provides a set of input numbers and a target integer, and requires an arithmetic expression over + + , − - , × \times , ÷ \div that uses each input number exactly once and evaluates to the target. The data provide fixed ordered difficulty groups indexed by n ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } n\in\{2,3,4,5\} , the number of input operands in the instance; larger n n increases the combinatorial search space and is empirically harder for the policy. We denote these preassigned groups by 𝒟 0 , … , 𝒟 K − 1 \mathcal{D}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{K-1} . The curriculum does not infer or relabel difficulty: at each step it samples a bucket k ∼ p t k\sim p_{t} and then samples an example uniformly from 𝒟 k \mathcal{D}_{k} . Exact-answer correctness is determined independently by the unchanged Countdown verifier. II-B Gaussian Curriculum Sampler The sampler follows the same Gaussian easy-to-hard form as the fixed E2H-G baseline [ 10 ] , which keeps the sampling family fixed and makes feedback the primary design difference between the two arms. The spread σ t \sigma_{t} controls rehearsal breadth: larger σ t \sigma_{t} flattens the distribution so neighboring buckets stay in the rollout mix. The additive floor p min > 0 p_{\min}>0 is applied to each unnormalized weight before normalization, guaranteeing every bucket retains nonzero probability; this keeps the hardest bucket from being starved entirely early in training while its share stays negligible until the controller deems it worthwhile. II-C Closed-Loop Curriculum Controller The controller closes the loop between the curriculum clock and the model’s observed competence using a fixed, non-learned feedback rule based on two inexpensive, interpretable signals. It remains anchored to the reference trajectory, reverting to the open-loop baseline when no corrective signal is present, and can be viewed as an RLVR-specific form of learning-progress-based automatic curriculum learning [ 5 , 9 ] . This probe is the only additional GPU computation introduced by ClosedLoopGaussian ; indicative timing is reported in § III . Controller parameters were coarsely calibrated to keep feedback responsive but bounded: h h and ℓ \ell were chosen from reference mid-training pass rates, while gains and clipping ranges were set conservatively to limit deviation from the E2H-G reference. Settings were then frozen before the reported comparison; seed 42 was used during calibration. All experiments use meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with LoRA fine-tuning. LoRA uses rank r = 32 r=32 , scale α LoRA = 64 \alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}=64 , and dropout 0.05 0.05 . Training runs for 1,600 1{,}600 optimizer steps with a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , cosine decay, and a 0.03 0.03 warm-up ratio. The per-device batch size is 4 4 with 4 4 gradient-accumulation steps. GRPO samples 4 4 generations per prompt with KL coefficient 0.001 0.001 and maximum gradient norm 1.0 1.0 . Generation and Probing. The maximum prompt and completion lengths are 1,024 1{,}024 and 192 192 tokens, respectively. Training generations use temperature 0.7 0.7 and top- p = 1.0 p=1.0 . Controller probes are performed every Δ = 100 \Delta=100 optimizer steps using a fixed set of 100 100 examples from each difficulty bucket and greedy decoding. Periodic probing introduces additional inference cost; in one representative run, ClosedLoopGaussian required 12.94 h versus 11.49 h for Fixed E2H-G and 10.82 h for GRPO, although these single-run timings are indicative only. Controller Configuration. The controller uses reference values β ref = 0.50 \beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.50 and σ ref = 0.50 \sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.50 , with probability floor p min = 0.01 p_{\min}=0.01 . The controller variables are bounded by β ∈ [ 0.35 , 0.70 ] \beta\in[0.35,0.70] and σ ∈ [ 0.40 , 0.80 ] \sigma\in[0.40,0.80] . III-B Accuracy Across Difficulty Levels Across four seeds, average exact-match accuracy is 42.4 % ± 14.0 % 42.4\%\pm 14.0\% for ClosedLoopGaussian , 35.0 % ± 11.4 % 35.0\%\pm 11.4\% for Fixed E2H-G, and 26.4 % ± 21.6 % 26.4\%\pm 21.6\% for GRPO (Table I ). Across difficulty levels, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN achieves mean accuracies of 82.7%, 52.3%, 23.2%, and 11.5% for n = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 n=2,3,4,5 , respectively, compared with 73.1%, 40.8%, 16.3%, and 9.7% for Fixed E2H-G. ClosedLoopGaussian exceeds Fixed E2H-G on all four reported seeds, but the across-seed dispersion is large relative to the mean gaps; with only n = 4 n=4 seeds, the comparison does not support a statistical-significance claim and is therefore interpreted descriptively. The largest mean gains over Fixed E2H-G occur at difficulty n = 3 n=3 ( 52.3 % 52.3\% vs. 40.8 % 40.8\% ) and n = 4 n=4 ( 23.2 % 23.2\% vs. 16.3 % 16.3\% ), consistent with adaptation being most useful where rollouts are neither uniformly correct nor uniformly incorrect. Each bucket contains 250 250 evaluation problems, so one example corresponds to 0.4 0.4 percentage points; small differences at n = 5 n=5 therefore represent only a few examples and should not be overinterpreted. Figure 2 traces β t \beta_{t} , σ t \sigma_{t} , u β u_{\beta} , and n = 3 n=3 probe accuracy across all four seeds. The first probe at step 100 100 shows near-floor accuracy beyond the easiest bucket, producing a mildly negative u β u_{\beta} and a small increase in β t \beta_{t} above its 0.5 0.5 reference. After warm-up, two qualitative regimes emerge. On seeds 42 42 , 43 43 , and 1 1 , n = 3 n=3 probe accuracy rises, u β u_{\beta} becomes positive, and β t \beta_{t} decreases toward approximately 0.35 0.35 – 0.40 0.40 , shifting progression toward harder buckets; σ t \sigma_{t} remains near its reference with only modest widening. Seed 43 43 shows the strongest acceleration and the highest final accuracy, while seed 1 1 exhibits a transient mid-training dip before returning to the acceleration regime. Seed 44 44 follows a different trajectory: n = 3 n=3 competence remains low, u β u_{\beta} returns to zero after step 200 200 , and β t \beta_{t} relaxes near the reference, while forgetting on easier buckets widens σ t \sigma_{t} to approximately 0.63 0.63 . This near-reference β t \beta_{t} is the intended reference-anchoring behavior when no pace-adjustment signal is present. The fixed controller therefore exhibits either accelerated progression or increased rehearsal depending on the observed probe trajectory. As a single-seed auxiliary analysis, seed 43 43 sampler logs show that the closed-loop schedule assigns 6.45 6.45 percentage points more sampling mass to n = 5 n=5 than Fixed E2H-G, with the shift drawn primarily from n = 3 n=3 and n = 4 n=4 . Notably, n = 3 n=3 accuracy improves despite receiving less n = 3 n=3 training exposure, suggesting that the gain cannot be explained simply by sampling that bucket more frequently. Dashed grey lines mark the reference values ( β ref = σ ref = 0.5 \beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.5 , u β = 0 u_{\beta}=0 ). Seeds 42 42 / 43 43 / 1 1 move ahead of pace and the controller accelerates the curriculum ( β t ↓ \beta_{t}\!\downarrow ); seed 44 44 never gets ahead, u β u_{\beta} stays at zero, and the controller instead widens the distribution ( σ t ↑ \sigma_{t}\!\uparrow ) to counter forgetting. III-D Diagnostic Sensitivity to Controller Authority Seed 43 43 is examined because it exhibits the largest controller movement, making sensitivity to controller authority easiest to observe. This seed was selected after inspecting the controller trajectories, so the analysis is post hoc and is reported as a diagnostic rather than a representative ablation. On this seed, locking σ = 0.50 \sigma=0.50 reduces average accuracy from 58.9 58.9 to 26.2 26.2 , indicating that spread adaptation can matter for this trajectory. Pace-bound changes also produce substantial variation, with the default [ 0.35 , 0.70 ] [0.35,0.70] band outperforming both tighter and wider alternatives; this band was fixed before the reported runs (§ II-C ) and was not selected on the basis of these evaluation results. Because this diagnostic uses one selected seed and omits the complementary β \beta -locked/ σ \sigma -active condition, it does not establish an average contribution of σ \sigma or a causal decomposition of pace and spread. III-E Seed-Dependent Stability The large standard deviations in Table I are consistent with training instability in the underlying GRPO optimization rather than by the curriculum. Vanilla GRPO is the least stable arm: it collapses to near-floor accuracy on two of the four seeds ( 44 44 and 1 1 , both 7.7 % 7.7\% ) while reaching 43 43 – 47 % 47\% on the other two, so its variance is bimodal rather than Gaussian and its mean of 26.4 % 26.4\% should be read with that in mind. These two seeds are separate runs with their own output directories and independently written checkpoints; their identical per-bucket accuracies reflect two runs reaching the same near-floor outcome, not a duplicated result entry. The curriculum arms avoided near-floor outcomes on the same initializations: Fixed E2H-G never falls below 19.2 % 19.2\% , and ClosedLoopGaussian never below 25.1 % 25.1\% . We therefore treat seed 44 44 not as an outlier to be averaged away but as a documented stability observation, and seed 1 1 shows the same effect for GRPO a second time: closed-loop adaptation provides a measure of robustness to an unfavorable optimization trajectory precisely because its pace and spread react to the model’s deteriorating competence. At the same time, we are explicit that with four seeds on a single 3 3 B model and a single task, these results give a consistent ordering and a mechanistic account , not a tight quantitative estimate of the expected gain. IV Limitations and Future Directions This study focuses on a controlled setting: a single 3 3 B model (Llama-3.2-3B with LoRA), a single task (Countdown), and four seeds. The broader model, task, and seed coverage would further refine quantitative estimates of the expected gain, especially given the seed-to-seed variation observed in § III-E . Direct experimental comparisons with adaptive curricula such as AdaRFT, DUMP, and SEC are also left for future work. The controller’s effectiveness also depends on the choice of thresholds and control gains. Controller thresholds, gains, and bounds are manually calibrated; overly strict settings can cause curriculum deadlock, although the reference-anchored bounded design mitigates this failure mode. Future work should expand seed and domain coverage, compare directly with adaptive-curriculum baselines, and automate controller calibration from training signals. V Conclusion This work studied when closed-loop curriculum adaptation improves reinforcement fine-tuning for LLM reasoning. We introduced ClosedLoopGaussian , a feedback-driven curriculum scheduler for GRPO that treats training-time data selection as an adaptive decision problem. Rather than changing the reward function, model architecture, or GRPO optimizer, ClosedLoopGaussian reallocates a fixed rollout budget across difficulty buckets using periodic probe estimates of per-bucket accuracy. It achieved higher mean exact-match accuracy than fixed E2H-G and vanilla GRPO across four reported seeds, although seed-to-seed variation is substantial. More broadly, this study highlights the value of decision-guided training mechanisms that improve reasoning by changing how compute is allocated, rather than by increasing model size or redesigning the optimizer, establishing closed-loop curriculum scheduling as a lightweight and transparent component for building more efficient AI training systems.
